Listen to this article Share Tanzania has discovered an estimated 223 billion cubic feet of natural gas in the Mnazi Bay area, its first new find in more than a decade, as the East African country seeks to expand domestic energy supply to meet rising electricity and industrial demand. The discovery was made at the Kasa-1X ST2 well in the southern Mtwara region through a partnership between state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) and French oil and gas company Maurel & Prom, according to international reports. The well is expected to begin production as early as November 2026, adding to supplies from the existing Mnazi Bay field, where gas is already used to generate electricity and support industrial activities. According to Maurel & Prom, the discovery contains an estimated 200 billion cubic feet of gas on a gross basis, or about 120 billion cubic feet attributable to its 60 percent interest in the license. The company said the well could produce up to 50 million cubic feet per day. Read also: Nigeria’s domestic economy will benefit from stronger links to its vast gas reserves The Tanzanian government has put the discovery at 223 billion cubic feet, equivalent to about 6.3 billion cubic metres. Juma Zuberi Homera, Tanzania’s energy minister, described the find as a “major milestone”, saying it would help strengthen domestic supply as demand increases alongside industrial expansion and other economic activities. The discovery follows the drilling of three wells in the Mnazi Bay block, including Kasa-1X ST2, MB-5 and MS-2. The two development wells, MB-5 and MS-2, have already increased output by more than 65 million cubic feet per day, according to Homera. Maurel & Prom reported that production from the Mnazi Bay field had reached about 130 million cubic feet per day following the addition of the two wells. The latest discovery comes as Tanzania seeks to maximise the contribution of natural gas to its domestic energy market. The fuel accounted for nearly 80 percent of the country’s electricity generation in 2024. More than 80 percent of the gas produced at Mnazi Bay is used to generate electricity at Tanzania Electric Supply Company power plants in Mtwara and Dar es Salaam. Additional production could therefore strengthen supplies to the power sector while supporting other users, including industries and transport operators that have adopted compressed natural gas as a cheaper alternative to petrol. Tanzania has also been pursuing plans to expand the domestic use of gas beyond power generation. Homera said TPDC was in discussions with four investors interested in developing small-scale liquefied natural gas projects, three of which are expected to be located in Mtwara. The projects are intended to widen access to gas, create employment and support its use in vehicles as an alternative to petrol and diesel. However, the new find is relatively small compared with Tanzania’s existing gas resource base, estimated at 57.54 trillion cubic feet before the discovery. Its economic contribution will depend on the volume that can ultimately be recovered and the pace at which production is sustained. Tanzania’s gas industry developed from discoveries at Songo Songo Island in 1974 and Mnazi Bay in 1982. Commercial production began in 2004, paving the way for further exploration onshore and offshore. The country’s last reported gas discovery before the recent Kasa-1X ST2 was in 2015, more than a decade ago. The latest find adds to the country’s resource base, but its immediate significance lies in the prospect of increasing output from an established producing area, where existing infrastructure and demand could facilitate the supply of additional gas to the domestic market.
